'''Mary Elizabeth Bartlett Bunge''' (April 3, 1931 – February 17, 2024) was an American [[neuroscientist]] who researched a cure for [[paralysis]] at the [[University of Miami]], where she was a professor of [[cell biology]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title = University of Miami Health System|url = http://uhealthsystem.com/researchers/profile/2588|website = uhealthsystem.com|access-date = November 30, 2015}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Mary Bartlett was born on April 3, 1931, in [[New Haven, Connecticut]], to George Chapman Bartlett and Margaret Elizabeth (Reynolds) Bartlett.<ref name="obit" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url = https://www.sfn.org/~/media/SfN/Documents/TheHistoryofNeuroscience/Volume%204/c2.ashx|title = The History of Neuroscience in Autobiography |editor1-last=Squire |editor1-first=Larry R.|date=2008 |publisher=Academic Press |location=San Diego |isbn=978-0-12-660246-3 |ol=7329095M }}</ref> Her father built and renovated houses, including the house in which she grew up, whereas her mother, a descendant of painter Sir [[Joshua Reynolds]], worked as a painter and decorator. Neither of her parents had a college education, and her father thought that a college education was useless for women. Their careers were filled with an artistic expression that Mary found appealing.<ref name=":1" />

After her grandmother taught her how to sew, she expressed herself through art and fashion by designing and making all of her own clothes with the ultimate dream to be a [[fashion design]]er in [[New York City]].<ref name=":1" /> She strongly considered a career in fashion design, but eventually decided her art interests could just be hobbies.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title = Mary Bartlett Bunge: A Life in Science, in Progress|url = http://www.christopherreeve.org/site/c.ddJFKRNoFiG/b.7711669/k.B763/Mary_Bartlett_Bunge_A_Life_in_Science_in_Progress.htm|website = Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation|access-date = November 30, 2015|archive-date = March 24, 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160324024506/http://www.christopherreeve.org/site/c.ddJFKRNoFiG/b.7711669/k.B763/Mary_Bartlett_Bunge_A_Life_in_Science_in_Progress.htm|url-status = dead}}</ref> She developed a passion for [[biology]] while she was observing the [[tadpole]]s swimming around her and questioned how they developed into [[frog]]s.<ref name=":2" />

== Education ==
Bartlett attended [[Simmons University|Simmons College]] in [[Boston]] to become a [[laboratory technician]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Pioneer">{{cite web |title="A True Neuroscience Pioneer:" Dr. Mary Bartlett Bunge Passes Away |url=https://news.med.miami.edu/mary-bartlett-bunge/ |publisher=[[Miller School of Medicine]] |access-date=February 21, 2024 |date=February 21, 2024}}</ref> At the end of her junior year at Simmons College, Bartlett was inspired to further her education while attending a program at [[Jackson Memorial Laboratory]], where she witnessed a rabbit's heart contract in a [[tissue culture]].<ref name=":1" /> This instance triggered the realization that she did not want to be a lab tech; she wanted to do research, so when she graduated from Simmons College in 1953, she accepted the invitation to graduate school at [[University of Wisconsin Medical School]] from Dr. Robert Schilling.<ref name=":1" /> He was a professor in the Department of Medical Physiology who offered Mary a research assistantship position when she was studying to obtain her master's degree.<ref name=":1" /> They researched [[intrinsic factor]], which is lacking from the [[gastric juices]] when one has the condition of [[pernicious anemia]] and cannot absorb [[vitamin B12]].<ref name=":1" /> Their research had a clinical relevance that influenced her later research to be focused toward clinical applications.<ref name=":1" /> This work was the basis of her [[thesis]], which allowed her to graduate with her master's degree in medical physiology in 1955.<ref name=":1" />

While studying for her doctorate at the [[University of Wisconsin Medical School]], Mary worked in the zoology department with Dr. [[Hans Ris]].<ref name=":1" /> She graduated with her doctorate in 1960.<ref name=":1" />

== Academic career and research ==
Bunge and her husband Richard graduated together from the University of Wisconsin Medical School and moved to [[Columbia University]] to begin their post-doctorate research.<ref name=":1" /> Bunge worked part-time for eight years as a research associate at Columbia University.<ref name=":1" />

In 1970, Bunge and her family moved to accept faculty positions at [[Washington University School of Medicine]].<ref name=":1" /> She chose to be a research assistant professor rather than be on the [[tenure-track]] so she could continue raising her sons, who were still young.<ref name=":1" /> She also adjusted to a full-time schedule.<ref name=":1" /> By 1974, she had started to teach and was promoted to associate professor with [[tenure]].<ref name=":1" /> She was promoted again in 1978 to professor.<ref name=":1" />

Richard enriched Bunge's life by introducing her to [[neuroscience]], where she found her purpose and focused her research on while at Washington University School of Medicine.<ref name=":1" /> In particular, she focused on researching [[Schwann cell]]s, which are cells that wrap around the [[axon]] of [[neurons]] to form the [[myelin]] sheath as an insulator to the [[neuron]] and to increase the speed impulses are conducted.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Pioneer"/> One of her other major discoveries was that the [[oligodendrocyte]] was the cell that made the myelin sheath for the [[central nervous system]].<ref name=":1" /> She first discovered this when she examined a section of a kitten's spinal cord in an [[electron microscope]] with the oligodendrocyte cell body forming myelin at each end.<ref name=":1" /> She also demonstrated that myelin could be reformed in the mature mammalian spinal cord, which has an important clinical relevance in addressing [[multiple sclerosis]] and [[Spinal cord injury|spinal cord injuries]], where the myelin has been damaged.<ref name=":1" />

Between 1989 and 2023, Bunge was a leading part of the [[Miami Project to Cure Paralysis]] at the [[Miller School of Medicine|University of Miami School of Medicine]], where her research on myelin has been implemented.<ref name=":5" /> Her husband was invited to be the scientific director of the project, so she was able to work with him there, and when he died in 1996 from [[esophageal cancer]], she took his place at the forefront of the project.<ref name=":2" /> The project Bunge took over tests regeneration strategies that could lead to successful treatment of [[spinal cord injury]].<ref name=":5" />

Bunge had the [[patent]] in "Schwann Cell Bridge Implants and [[Phosphodiesterase]] Inhibitors to Stimulate CNS Nerve Regeneration" from 2009 for the application of restoring function after a central nervous system injury.<ref>{{Cite web|title = US20090136463.pdf|url = https://docs.google.com/viewer?url=patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/pdfs/US20090136463.pdf|website = docs.google.com|access-date = December 1, 2015}}</ref> She has dozens of other [[patent]]s including "Methods and Systems for Neural Maintenance and Regeneration,"<ref>{{Cite web|title = US8267920.pdf|url = https://docs.google.com/viewer?url=patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/pdfs/US8267920.pdf|website = docs.google.com|access-date = December 1, 2015}}</ref> "Promoters of Neural Regeneration,"<ref>{{Cite web|title = US20030134821.pdf|url = https://docs.google.com/viewer?url=patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/pdfs/US20030134821.pdf|website = docs.google.com|access-date = December 1, 2015}}</ref> and "Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors for Cognitive and Motor Rehabilitation."<ref>{{Cite web|title = EP2377533A2.pdf|url = https://docs.google.com/viewer?url=patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/pdfs/1919bd543e95ffc207f6/EP2377533A2.pdf|website = docs.google.com|access-date = December 1, 2015}}</ref> Her research was used for phase one of clinical trials, which gained approval from the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] in 2012, to evaluate the safety of transplanting the Schwann cells of recently paralyzed patients into the site of their injury.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|title = In the News – The Miami Project to Cure Paralysis|url = http://www.miamiproject.miami.edu/page.aspx?pid=1180|website = www.miamiproject.miami.edu|access-date = December 1, 2015|archive-date = September 10, 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150910004738/http://www.miamiproject.miami.edu/page.aspx?pid=1180|url-status = dead}}</ref>

While the trial occurred, Bunge worked on other combination treatments for future clinical trials.<ref name=":7" /> In 2014, she published in ''[[The Journal of Neuroscience]]'' the promising results of a strategy tested in rat Schwann cells that were engineered to secrete the growth factor D15A and the enzyme [[Chondroitinase ABC|Chondroitinase]] ABC which alters scar composition.<ref name=":7" /> This combination led to more axonal regeneration and functional improvement.<ref name=":7" />

== Honors ==
Bunge was a professor of [[cell biology]], [[neurological surgery]], and [[neurology]] at the [[University of Miami]] for more than two decades and received recognition for her research.<ref name=":5" /> In 1996, she received the Wakeman Award for Spinal Cord Repair.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Mary Bartlett Bunge Elected to Institute of Medicine |url=http://www.miami.edu/index.php/news/releases/mary_bartlett_bunge_elected_to_institute_of_medicine/ |access-date=November 30, 2015 |website=miami.edu |publisher=University of Miami}}</ref> She was a three time recipient of the Javitis Neuroscience Investigator Award from the [[National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke]].<ref name=":6" />

She was the elected Chair of the Development of Women's Careers in Neuroscience Committee through the [[Society for Neuroscience]] from 1994 to 2002. In 2000, she received the Mika Salpeter Women In Neuroscience Lifetime Achievement Award for her leadership in advancing the careers of women in neuroscience.<ref name=":6" />

In 2001, she received the Christopher Reeve Research Medal for Spinal Cord Repair.<ref name=":6" /> She received the Christine E Lynn Distinguished Professor in Neuroscience Award in 2003 and the [[Lois Pope]] LIFE International Research Award in 2005.<ref name=":6" /> She was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] Institute of Medicine.<ref name=":6" />

== Personal life ==
While at the University of Wisconsin Medical School, she met a medical student named Richard Bunge, whom she married and shared her personal and career lives with.<ref name=":2" /> Soon after settling in at Columbia University, they had two sons, Jonathan, born in 1962, and Peter, born in 1964.<ref name=":2" />

Bunge died in [[Coral Gables, Florida]] on February 17, 2024, at the age of 92.<ref name="Pioneer"/><ref name="obit">{{cite web|title=Mary Bartlett Bunge, 92, Dies; Pioneer in Spinal Injury Treatment|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/04/science/mary-bartlett-bunge-dead.html|date=March 4, 2024|last=Risen|first=Clay|work=The New York Times|access-date=March 5, 2024}}</ref>
